big: Four funds can all be called equity funds and still be built in very different ways. The name sets the allowed range. The factsheet shows what is really inside.

lines: I want just one equity fund. Which type should it be?
Let us see how the main types are allowed to be built, and what that means for her.

rows.name: Flexi cap fund
segs: Any mix of large, mid and small cap stocks

rows.name: Focused fund (at most 30 stocks)
segs: Any mix, but only 30 stocks or fewer

alt: Bars showing how a multi cap, a flexi cap and a focused fund are built
caps: A multi cap fund must keep at least 25% each in large, mid and small caps.
A flexi cap fund has no minimum for each bucket, so the manager has the most freedom.
A focused fund holds at most 30 stocks. A wrong pick hurts more.

q: What must a multi cap fund hold at the minimum?
opts: At least 25% each in large, mid and small caps
At least 80% in large caps and the rest in mid caps
why: Three buckets at 25% each adds up to 75%. The remaining 25% is left to the manager's choice.
The 80% large cap floor belongs to a large cap fund. A multi cap fund must spread across all three buckets.
The 65% small cap floor belongs to a small cap fund. A multi cap fund cannot be all small caps.
No such floor exists for mid caps in a multi cap fund. The rule sets a floor for each of the three buckets.

q: A client wants one equity fund for her core money and is comfortable trusting the manager. What is a reasonable choice?
opts: A sectoral fund, since one sector is simple to follow
A flexi cap fund, with a yearly check of what it actually holds
A focused fund of 10 stocks, since fewer stocks means less risk
A small cap fund, because it can grow the fastest
why: A sector fund holds one corner of the market. It can fall hard for years when that corner is out of favour.
A manager who can move across all caps suits a one-fund core, and the yearly check catches drift from her comfort.
Fewer stocks means each one matters more. A mistake in one name can hurt the whole fund.
Small caps have deep falls. As a single fund it carries more risk than a one-fund core should.

q: Which statement about a focused fund is correct?
opts: It holds at most 30 stocks, so one wrong stock hurts more
It must hold at least 30 stocks, which makes it safer
It invests only in large caps, with no mid caps
It can hold any number of stocks, like a flexi cap fund
why: The limit is a maximum. With few stocks, the weight of each one is larger and a single failure shows in the NAV.
The number is a ceiling, not a floor. A focused fund with a high floor would not be focused at all.
A focused fund can hold stocks from any bucket. The rule limits the count, not the size of the companies.
The cap of 30 is what makes the fund focused. A flexi cap fund has no such limit on the number of stocks.

q: The fund's name says flexi cap. Where do you check how much of it is in small caps today?
opts: The fund's name, since it states the exact mix of the fund
The factsheet, which shows the real mix by market cap
The NAV chart, which shows the mix by the colour of its line
The exit load table in the offer document of the scheme
why: A name sets the range the fund may use. Two flexi cap funds can hold quite different mixes inside it.
The factsheet lists the real mix by market cap, and the portfolio shows each stock. It is the place to look.
A NAV chart shows price over time only. It carries no information about what the fund holds.
The exit load says what you pay to leave early. It tells you nothing about the stocks inside.

pts: Multi cap: at least 25% each in large, mid and small. Flexi cap: any mix. Focused: at most 30 stocks.
Flexi cap suits one core fund, if you trust the manager.
The label sets the range. The factsheet shows the truth, so check it every year.
